title: UTF-8 Validation
statement:
Each value in `data` is one byte (an integer from 0 to 255). Return `true` if the bytes, read from left to right, split completely into valid UTF-8 characters, and `false` otherwise.

A UTF-8 character is 1 to 4 bytes long:

- A 1-byte character is a single byte whose highest bit is `0` (pattern `0xxxxxxx`).
- An n-byte character, for n = 2, 3 or 4, starts with a byte whose top n bits are all `1` and whose next bit is `0` (`110xxxxx`, `1110xxxx` or `11110xxx`). It is followed by exactly n - 1 continuation bytes, each with top two bits `10` (`10xxxxxx`).

An `x` can be either bit. Every byte must belong to exactly one character, so a character cut short by the end of `data` makes the whole input invalid.
notes:
## Intuition

Only the first byte of a character says how long the character is; every byte after it must look like a continuation byte. So one left-to-right pass is enough if we remember a single number: how many continuation bytes the current character still needs. A byte's top bits are read by shifting it right, e.g. `byte >> 5` keeps only its top three bits.

## Approach

1. Set `remaining = 0`: no character is in progress.
2. For each `byte`: if `remaining > 0`, it must be a continuation byte (`byte >> 6` equals `0b10`); if not, return `false`, otherwise decrease `remaining`.
3. If no character is in progress, `byte` starts one. Test the patterns from shortest to longest: `byte >> 7 === 0` is a 1-byte character; `byte >> 5 === 0b110` needs 1 more byte, `byte >> 4 === 0b1110` needs 2, `byte >> 3 === 0b11110` needs 3.
4. Any other leading byte (a stray `10xxxxxx`, or five or more leading ones) is invalid: return `false`.
5. After the loop, return whether `remaining` is `0`, so that the last character was not cut short.

## Example 1, step by step

`data = [197, 130, 1]`. `197` is `11000101`; `197 >> 5 = 6 = 0b110`, so `remaining = 1`. `130` is `10000010`; `130 >> 6 = 2 = 0b10`, a continuation, so `remaining = 0`. `1` is `00000001`; `1 >> 7 = 0`, a 1-byte character. The loop ends with `remaining = 0`, so the answer is `true`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n), one constant-time check per byte.
- Space: O(1), only the counter `remaining`.

## Pitfalls

- Compare the whole prefix, including its `0` bit: `byte >> 5 === 0b110` is right, but `(byte & 0b11000000) === 0b11000000` would also accept `1110xxxx` as the start of a 2-byte character.
- A continuation byte (`10xxxxxx`) cannot start a character; it must be rejected when `remaining` is `0`.
- Bytes with five or more leading ones (248 and above) are never valid.
- Return `remaining === 0`, not `true`: input like `[240, 162, 138]` ends in the middle of a character.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `byte` | the current value of `data` |
| `remaining` | continuation bytes the current character still needs |

narration.2: No character is in progress yet, so no continuation bytes are owed.
narration.3: Read the bytes from left to right.
narration.4: A character has started and still needs continuation bytes.
narration.5: Shifting right by 6 keeps the top two bits, which must be 10.
narration.6: Anything else breaks the current character.
narration.8: One continuation byte fewer is still owed.
narration.11: Top bits 110: a 2-byte character, so one continuation byte must follow.
narration.13: Top bits 1110: a 3-byte character needing two more bytes.
narration.15: Top bits 11110: a 4-byte character needing three more bytes.
narration.18: A stray continuation byte or five leading ones cannot start a character.
narration.21: Valid only if the last character was not cut off by the end of data.
